run_metadata.seed_myth:
Myth: In the time before patience was valued, there lived a potter named Maren whose kiln required seven firings to complete a single vessel. Other potters finished their work in one firing, selling quickly and abundantly.

"Why waste time on what yields so little?" the guild asked, watching her tedious process.

But Maren understood what haste would break. Each firing revealed new flaws—a bubble here, a weakness there. She would repair, refire, and wait. Her vessels took seasons to complete, but they never cracked under pressure, never leaked when filled.

One drought came when the village wells ran dry. The quick-fired vessels, beautiful but fragile, shattered when carried long distances to distant springs. The villagers' water spilled uselessly into dust.

Maren brought forth her seven-fired vessels. "Take these," she said. "They were made for endurance, not speed."

The villagers carried water from distant mountains. Maren's vessels survived every journey, their patient construction proving stronger than rushed perfection. The village survived the drought.

The guild masters came to her workshop. "Teach us your method," they requested.

"Gladly," Maren replied, "but first you must learn to wait."

This is why slow building outlasts quick promises. Maren showed that what endures is worth the time it takes to create properly.
